text:
I'm going to speak at our county planning commission tonight in favor of a housing project, and I want help writing what I'll say. The church I belong to wants to build 64 apartments on its back parking lot. All of them would rent to households earning under 60% of the area median income.

Facts:
- The church lot is 1.8 acres and sits empty 6 days a week.
- The county's own housing report says we are short about 2,100 affordable homes.
- The traffic study estimates 310 more car trips a day on Alder Road, and says the intersection at Alder and 4th would drop from a C rating to a D at rush hour.
- The plan has 72 parking spaces for the 64 units.
- 412 households are on the county housing authority's waiting list. The average wait is 3 years.
- I've lived on Alder Road for 19 years, two blocks from the church.

Each speaker gets 3 minutes.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will decide how the speech handles the hardest parts.

1. **What's the main objection you expect tonight?** Is it traffic on Alder, parking spillover, density, or something else? And do you know whether the commissioners themselves have raised any concerns? Three minutes only covers one objection properly, so I want to pick the right one.
2. **Is anything planned to fix the Alder and 4th intersection?** For example, retimed signals, a turn lane, or a condition of approval. If not, I'll address the C-to-D drop honestly rather than skip it. Someone else will bring it up if you don't.
3. **Is there a personal story you'd be comfortable telling?** For example, someone you know who is on the waiting list or who was priced out of the area, or what you've seen of Alder Road over 19 years. One real person usually lands better than a fourth statistic.
4. **What exactly is the commission voting on tonight?** Is it a rezoning, a variance, a site plan or something else? And are you asking them to approve it as proposed or with conditions? The closing ask should match the decision in front of them.
5. **Do you want to say up front that you're a member of the church?** I'd recommend it, since commissioners or opponents may already know and it builds trust to say it first. But it's your call.

If you don't know some of these, that's fine. I'll write without them.

1. Probably traffic on Alder. I don't know if the commissioners have raised anything themselves.

2. Yes. The builder, Cascade Housing Partners, has offered to pay for a traffic signal at Alder and 4th. The traffic study says with the signal the intersection stays at C.

3. Not someone on the waiting list. But I can say that some mornings around 8, traffic on Alder already backs up past my house.

4. It's the permit. I want them to approve it with the traffic signal as a condition. I don't know the exact type of permit.

5. Yes, I'll say it up front. The church is St. Luke's Lutheran.

<final_document>
Good evening, commissioners. My name is [your name]. I've lived on Alder Road for 19 years, two blocks from St. Luke's Lutheran. I'm also a member of St. Luke's, and I wanted you to know that up front.

I'm here to ask you to approve the permit for 64 affordable apartments on the church's back parking lot, with a traffic signal at Alder and 4th as a condition of approval.

I'll start with traffic, because I know that's what many of my neighbors are worried about, and I understand why. Some mornings around 8, traffic on Alder already backs up past my house. I'm not going to tell you that 310 more trips a day won't matter.

But the traffic study answers that worry. Without changes, the intersection at Alder and 4th would drop from a C to a D at rush hour. Cascade Housing Partners has offered to pay for a signal there. With that signal, the study says the intersection stays at a C. So this project doesn't have to make things worse for those of us who live on Alder, as long as the signal actually gets built. That's why I'm asking you to make it a condition, not just leave it as an offer.

On parking, the plan has 72 spaces for 64 units, which is more than one space per apartment.

Now, why this project matters. The county's own housing report says we are short about 2,100 affordable homes. Right now, 412 households are on the housing authority's waiting list, and the average wait is three years. Every one of these 64 apartments would rent to a household earning under 60 percent of the area median income. Those are exactly the families who are waiting.

And the site makes sense. It's 1.8 acres of parking lot that sits empty six days a week. Nothing gets torn down and no open land gets paved. We'd be putting land that's mostly unused to good use.

I've lived in this neighborhood for 19 years, and I believe it has room for 64 more households. That's especially true with a signal that keeps our busiest intersection at the rating it has today.

Please approve this permit, with the traffic signal at Alder and 4th as a condition. Thank you.
</final_document>

**Before tonight:**
- **Length:** The speech is about 390 words, which runs a little under 3 minutes at a calm pace. Time yourself reading it out loud once. If you run long, cut the parking paragraph first.
- **Check the signal offer:** If you can, make sure Cascade's offer to pay for the signal is in the staff report or the application. If a commissioner asks, you'll want to say where it's written down.
- **What I didn't add:** You didn't know the permit type, so the speech just says "the permit." I also didn't claim the parking will keep cars off Alder. The 72-for-64 figure supports that, but nothing you gave me proves it. If staff or the builder has said so on the record, you can add it.
